newsitem.title: UK: British film makers await news of lottery winners.
newsitem.headline: British film makers await news of lottery winners.

text.p: British film makers on Thursday were eagerly waiting to find out whether they would be among the winners of nearly 160 million pounds ($262.8 million) of national lottery funds.

The Arts Council of England planned to pick four winners out of some 37 groups bidding for the franchises, which were aimed at boosting local financing for films and nurturing a mini studio system in Britain.
The independent arts group expected to announce the winners at 1500 GMT at a news conference at the Cannes Film Festival.
Under the plan, each group would receive up to 39 million pounds over the next six years to help finance a range of films.
This unprecendented sum marked a sharp increase from the estimated 30 million pounds of lottery funds invested by the Arts Council in films over the past two years.
The financing was expected to help break down one of the main barriers to the British film industry's development -- the lack of local financing for movies.

"This is a new source of equity funding for British film producers, and funding has been in very short supply over the last few years," said Charles Denton, chairman of the Arts Council's film panel, in a recent interview.
Although British-themed films have staged a revival in recent years, many of the biggest hits, such as "The English Patient", got their financing from overseas.
This means that profits from the films return to their foreign investors, who may decide to use the money elsewhere rather than re-invest it in Britain.

The Arts Council planned to counteract this cycle by investing in groups that could produce and distribute a sizeable slate of films, thus enabling them to offset production costs with profits from distribution.
"Over years -- and it will be a question of years -- you might see the emergence of mini-studios," Denton said.

"Not on the kind of scale that you have in the U.S., but on a scale which would provide a base for British film makers and new talent rather than constantly having to start at the bottom of the hill with every individual film," he added.

The plan drew bids from a number of heavy hitters, including a group formed by Merchant Ivory Production, investment bank Guinness Mahon, EMI Music Publishing and pop singer Elton John's Rocket Pictures.
Bidding for the franchises was not restricted to local firms, but winners would be required to produce films that qualify as "British" in terms of location, work crews, and other criteria.
The Arts Council planned to invest in films on a minority basis, with lottery funding capped at about 2.0 million pounds or one-third of the movie's budget.
The financing was intended to act as seed money to attract other investors.

"A number of the applicants have been able to use the prospect of Arts Council funding to leverage in financial institutions and banks who have looked extremely sceptically at the British film industry," Denton said.
The funds will be invested on a film-by-film basis, with the Arts Council reserving veto powers over the financing.
"This gives the Arts Council a lever -- if you like, a weapon -- to be absolutely sure that the promises made by franchiseholders are met," Denton said.
Although British film makers generally praised the plan, some critics dismissed it as a subsidy that was unlikely to produce marketable movies.
But the Arts Council argued that the lottery funds are an investment rather than a grant or subsidy.
"The Arts Council has an expectation -- however that may be met, only time will tell -- of recoupment and indeed sharing in net profits," Denton said. ($ = 0.608 British Pounds)
